Visual Art encompasses creative works made primarily for aesthetic contemplation and to be perceived through the eye: painting, sculpture, drawing, printmaking, photography, and other media. As a category distinct from performing or literary arts, it has flourished across all human cultures as a means of expression, ritual, documentation, and beauty-making, from the earliest cave paintings to contemporary installation art.

Visual art is broadly divided into traditional media like painting, sculpture, drawing, and printmaking, and contemporary practices including photography, video, digital art, performance art, installation, and conceptual art—a range continuously expanding with new technologies. The distinction between fine art and applied art emerged as an eighteenth-century Western concept tied to aesthetic value systems, though modern art theory has blurred the historical boundaries between visual art, craft, and decorative arts.

The Renaissance, a cultural revolution centered in Italian cities like Florence, rediscovered perspective, anatomy, and classical ideals through visual media, fundamentally transforming how humans represented the world and themselves. Central to Modernism were radical experiments with abstraction, color theory, fragmentation, and the outright rejection of representational realism in movements like Cubism, Surrealism, and Abstract Expressionism, fundamentally challenging what art could be and opening entirely new possibilities for creative expression.

Visual art is analyzed and theorized through formal properties like composition, color, form, and line, as well as through meaning and iconography, making it a rich site for both creative practice and scholarly interpretation across disciplines. It serves as a vehicle for cultural memory, identity, and power, reflecting and shaping how societies understand themselves, their values, and their place in history, from ancient temple reliefs to contemporary installations.

Unlike literature or music, visual art requires active interpretation and direct engagement through the eye, inviting embodied presence that makes the viewer's position in front of the work part of its meaning. This direct visual engagement is fundamental to the experience of art itself.
